periods.analysis: IT Service Desk resolution time closed 2024-Q3 at 6.6 hours, safely inside the <=8.0-hour green target and establishing a controlled baseline for the new reporting series. With no prior-quarter comparator, I am treating this as a starting control point rather than a victory lap. The strongest contributors were same-day closure of password, MFA, and printer queue tickets on the Civic Center and Harborview Library routes, while endpoint imaging requests remained the main source of age risk. The result is consistent with a healthy operating posture, provided we keep measuring the queue by ticket age and not just average speed.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the current triage model by keeping the 8:15 a.m. ServiceNow aging review and assigning named owners to every ticket over 6 hours. Extend the green performance by piloting a 20-device spare-laptop pool for Finance, HR, and Community Development, where downtime carries higher business-continuity risk. Continue weekly quality checks on closed tickets to confirm that speed is not being achieved by premature closure.

periods.analysis: Resolution time rose to 7.8 hours in 2024-Q4, a 1.2-hour increase from 6.6 hours, but remained green against the <=8.0-hour target. The movement was expected and manageable, driven by year-end account changes, police mobile-device certificate renewals, and the Tyler ERP patch window that generated a short-lived batch of access tickets. I do not see a control failure, but the margin to target narrowed to 0.2 hours, which is close enough to warrant disciplined monitoring. The team kept the queue stable by using the holiday coverage roster and routing after-hours VPN issues directly to the network on-call technician.
periods.recommendations: Keep the holiday coverage playbook, but add a formal trigger: if the rolling three-day average exceeds 7.5 hours, the desktop and applications leads should run a same-day backlog scrub. Extend the green result by pre-staging Q4 access-change templates for seasonal recreation, finance close, and public safety certificate renewals. Audit a sample of December closures to verify that recurring ERP and VPN issues are being converted into knowledge articles rather than repeated one-off fixes.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q1, resolution time improved to 7.0 hours, a 0.8-hour decrease from 7.8 hours, keeping the measure green and restoring more operating room below the <=8.0-hour standard. The improvement followed tighter intake coding in ServiceNow and a January cleanup of duplicate tickets from the email-to-ticket connector. We also saw benefit from assigning the Municipal Services Building and North Harbor Public Works yard to fixed technician routes on Tuesdays and Thursdays. From a risk perspective, the result is positive, but access-management tickets still need clean documentation because they affect auditability as much as service speed.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the fixed-route model for Municipal Services and Public Works, and publish the route calendar so departments can batch lower-priority device work. Extend the gain by requiring the service desk to use standardized resolution codes for account unlocks, MFA resets, and permissions changes beginning next quarter. Perform a monthly access-ticket evidence review with Finance & Administration to ensure faster resolution remains aligned with control requirements.

periods.analysis: Resolution time improved again in 2025-Q2 to 5.9 hours, a 1.1-hour decrease from 7.0 hours and well within green performance. This is the best point in the series so far, and it appears supported by process changes rather than a temporary dip in demand. The new self-service password reset prompts, the Knowledge Base article set KB-145 through KB-153, and the spring workstation refresh schedule reduced avoidable hands-on work. I am comfortable with the trend, while still watching whether the low average masks a small number of older application tickets in permitting and payroll.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the self-service and knowledge-base gains by reviewing the top 15 ticket categories every two weeks and retiring outdated articles before they create control noise. Extend the green performance by adding QR-code links to approved help articles on shared workstations at City Hall, the marina office, and the community centers. Set a separate watch report for tickets older than 16 business hours so the strong average does not obscure unresolved high-risk items.

periods.analysis: The measure moved to 6.2 hours in 2025-Q3, a 0.3-hour increase from 5.9 hours, while remaining green against the <=8.0-hour target. The modest increase aligns with summer hiring, parks seasonal staff account provisioning, and added support for the online permit portal during peak construction activity. This is not a concerning movement, but it is a reminder that Harborview's growth creates more service-demand volatility even when the control environment is sound. The desk maintained queue discipline by using the intern-onboarding ticket bundle and separating permit-portal vendor escalations from standard desktop work.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the onboarding bundle for seasonal and temporary staff, including preapproved role templates for Parks, Marina Operations, and Recreation. Extend the green result by creating a dedicated permit-portal escalation code with the vendor so those tickets do not sit in the general queue while awaiting third-party action. Keep monitoring average resolution alongside backlog age, with specific review of any ticket that crosses the 8-hour target even if the quarterly average remains green.

periods.analysis: Resolution time increased to 7.6 hours in 2025-Q4, a 1.4-hour rise from 6.2 hours, but it remained green and below the <=8.0-hour target. The increase is material and expected given year-end procurement activity, cybersecurity awareness re-enrollment, and the Windows 11 compatibility remediation group for older inspection laptops. The team avoided a yellow result by scheduling evening imaging blocks and using the HarborTech managed-services bench for overflow during the final two weeks of December. My view is that performance is acceptable, but the control margin is again narrow and should be managed deliberately.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the evening imaging blocks for large endpoint waves, but require a daily exception log for devices that cannot be completed on schedule. Extend the green performance by pre-validating the 2026-Q1 replacement list for inspection laptops, police dock stations, and finance scanners before tickets are opened. Use HarborTech only under defined surge criteria, with ticket notes reviewed for completeness before vendor-assisted closures are accepted.

periods.analysis: In 2026-Q1, resolution time improved to 6.9 hours, a 0.7-hour decrease from 7.6 hours, returning a safer cushion under the <=8.0-hour target. The improvement reflects better sequencing of the Windows 11 remediation work and a cleaner handoff between the service desk and the infrastructure team for network-authentication incidents. The quarter also benefited from the new first-contact checklist for MFA, VPN, and mobile mail configuration, which reduced rework. I consider this a controlled improvement, with continued attention needed on documentation because fast fixes are not sufficient if they are not auditable.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the first-contact checklist and make it mandatory for MFA, VPN, mobile mail, and device-enrollment tickets. Extend the green performance by adding a quarterly tabletop review of high-volume incidents with Infrastructure, Cybersecurity, and HR onboarding leads. Continue sampling closed tickets for evidence quality, especially where access rights, privileged groups, or public-safety systems are involved.

periods.analysis: Resolution time reached 5.8 hours in 2026-Q2, a 1.1-hour decrease from 6.9 hours and the strongest performance in the eight-quarter arc. The result is firmly green against the <=8.0-hour target and suggests the service desk has converted earlier surge lessons into repeatable operating practice. The largest operational gains came from automated provisioning for the summer employment cohort, the refreshed laptop pool, and better vendor routing for the permitting and records systems. This is a strong outcome for a fast-growing city, but I would still avoid relaxing controls because volume and cyber-risk both tend to rise with scale.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the automated provisioning workflow and require HR to submit summer and temporary staff rosters at least 10 business days before start dates. Extend the green result by expanding the spare-device pool from the current pilot to Community Development, Public Works inspectors, and Police administration, with asset tags reconciled monthly. Preserve the control posture by keeping the 16-business-hour aging report and quarterly ticket-evidence review even while the average remains well below target.

periods.analysis: The available 5.8-hour resolution time is below the eight-hour ceiling. This is a carried-forward result, not a new September service-level improvement.
periods.recommendations: Retain the aging-ticket review and verify the September extract before reporting a trend.
